snip.t: Damage to podocytes or basement membrane produces haematuria and proteinuria, pointing to intrinsic glomerular disease.

qs.q: What urinalysis finding strongly suggests intrinsic AKI, particularly glomerular disease and acute tubular necrosis?
o: Hematuria, proteinuria, and red blood cell or granular casts
Absence of cellular elements with a high specific gravity
Isolated urinary eosinophils without protein or red cells
Presence of numerous bacteria without leukocyte casts
qs.e: The presence of hematuria, proteinuria, and red blood cell or granular urinary casts strongly points toward intrinsic AKI such as glomerular disease and ATN. An elevated specific gravity alone is more indicative of prerenal azotemia.

qs.q: What is the most accurate test used to establish a definitive diagnosis for suspected primary glomerular diseases?
qs.e: A kidney biopsy is the most accurate test to establish a diagnosis of primary glomerular disease based on histopathological characteristics. Urinalysis and blood tests are also used but biopsy is definitive.

qs.q: What is the most accurate test to establish a definitive diagnosis for a suspected primary glomerular disease?
qs.e: A biopsy is stated to be the most accurate test to establish a diagnosis of glomerular diseases, which are named based on histopathological characteristics. Urine collections are useful for quantification but do not provide histopathology.

qs.q: Which of the following medications are frequently used alongside corticosteroids to treat chronic glomerular diseases?
qs.e: Mycophenolate and cyclophosphamide are specifically mentioned as additional immunosuppressive medications frequently used to treat chronic glomerular diseases. Diuretics manage symptoms like edema but are not the primary immunosuppressive disease-modifying agents listed.

qs.q: Which anatomical components of the glomerulus are most likely to be targeted in nephritic glomerular disease due to their proximity to the blood circulation?
qs.e: The glomerular mesangium, endothelium, and GBM components are targeted in nephritic disease because of their proximity to blood circulation, leading to inflammation and hematuria. Podocytes are the primary target when nephrotic syndrome predominates.

qs.q: During the progression of glomerular disease, podocyte injury triggers a self-perpetuating cycle. Which of the following secondary changes almost always accompanies this progressive glomerular injury?
qs.e: Progressive glomerular injury is almost always accompanied by tubulointerstitial fibrosis as nephrons are lost and remaining structures undergo maladaptive changes. Tubulointerstitial scarring closely correlates with the decline in renal function.
qs.s: Glomerular Diseases: Classification, Histology & Pathology — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A 10-year-old child presents with chronic renal failure, haematuria, partial lipodystrophy, and retinal drusen. Serology confirms markedly low serum C3. What specific immunohistochemical finding distinguishes this patient's glomerular disease from MPGN Type I?
o: Presence of C3 staining alone without IgG, C1q, or C4
Granular subendothelial deposits of IgG along capillary loops
Positive staining for polyclonal IgG4 and kappa light chains
Dense linear staining of the glomerular basement membrane
qs.e: Dense deposit disease features C3 staining alone on immunofluorescence without IgG, C1q, or C4, which clearly distinguishes it from MPGN Type I where immune complexes yield IgG and C1q deposition. The presence of C3 alone reflects alternative pathway dysregulation rather than classical immune complex deposition.
qs.s: FSGS & HIV Nephropathy: Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis & Prognosis — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A pathologist identifies a specific co-chaperone for heat shock protein 70 within glomerular deposits as a sensitive and specific diagnostic marker for a rare glomerular disease that mimics amyloidosis. What is this marker protein?
qs.e: DNAJB9 has been identified as a highly sensitive and specific marker for fibrillary glomerulonephritis, found within its characteristic Congo red-negative deposits. Podocin and alpha-actinin 4 are structural podocyte proteins mutated in inherited forms of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Glomerular diseases are disorders of the kidney's filtering units that cause proteinuria, hematuria, or renal failure. Diagnosis relies on urine analysis, blood tests, and kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence or electron microscopy.

sections.p: Glomerular diseases affect the glomerular capillary wall, basement membrane, or mesangium, leading to abnormal filtration. Diagnosis starts with urinalysis, then blood chemistry, and is confirmed by kidney biopsy with IF/EM patterns.
b: Hematuria with red‑cell casts = glomerular bleed
Low serum complement (C3) suggests immune‑complex disease

t.b: Is there protein or blood? Detects nephrotic vs. nephritic patterns; dipstick positive for protein >300 mg/dL suggests glomerular leak.
How is kidney function? Rising creatinine indicates reduced filtration; guides urgency of referral.
What is the histologic pattern? Identifies minimal change, membranous, IgA nephropathy, etc.; essential for targeted therapy.

sections.p: Staging uses eGFR (KDIGO) and proteinuria level. Nephrotic syndrome is proteinuria >3.5 g/day; nephritic syndrome adds active urine sediment and impaired GFR.
Causes are grouped as primary (idiopathic) or secondary to systemic disease, infection, or drugs. In low‑resource settings, infections are common triggers.
Patients may have swelling, frothy urine, hypertension, or acute renal failure. Presentation differs between nephrotic (edema, hypoalbuminemia) and nephritic (hematuria, hypertension) patterns.
b: Facial puffiness and ascites in adults

sections.p: Beyond basic labs, targeted tests clarify etiology and severity, especially when biopsy is unavailable.

t.b: Is there immune‑complex activation? Low C3 suggests post‑infectious or lupus GN.

t.a: Serology for HIV, hepatitis B/C, malaria, schistosomiasis
t.b: Is a secondary infection present? Positive tests direct specific antimicrobial therapy.
Is membranous nephropathy likely? Positive result supports primary membranous disease.

t.a: If biopsy unavailable, use clinical algorithm (proteinuria + complement + serology) to approximate likely pathology.
t.b: Guides treatment when histology cannot be obtained.

sections.p: Complications arise from massive protein loss, hypertension, and progressive renal failure.
b: Rapid rise in creatinine (>30% in 48 h)
Severe hypoalbuminemia (<2 g/dL) with pulmonary edema

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control proteinuria, protect renal function, and manage complications. Use drugs with proven benefit and avoid those that worsen kidney injury.
b: Corticosteroids for minimal change disease or lupus GN – suppress immune inflammation.
Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) for steroid‑resistant nephrotic syndrome – reduce proteinuria.
ACE inhibitors or ARBs for all proteinuric patients – lower intraglomerular pressure and protein loss.
Antimicrobial therapy for identified infections (e.g., antiretrovirals for HIV, praziquantel for schistosomiasis).
Diuretics for edema – loop diuretics first line; avoid NSAIDs which worsen renal perfusion.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of kidney function, proteinuria, blood pressure, and lipid profile reduces long‑term damage.
b: Check eGFR and urine protein every 3‑6 months
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus

sections.p: Conditions that mimic glomerular disease can mislead clinicians.
Certain labs may appear normal despite serious disease.
b: Serum albumin may be normal early in nephrotic syndrome
Complement levels can be normal in IgA nephropathy
Urine dipstick may miss low‑molecular‑weight proteinuria

whenToSeekHelp: New onset hypertension with headache or visual changes

faq.q: Why does low C3 suggest an immune‑complex glomerulonephritis?
faq.a: Immune complexes activate complement, consuming C3; low levels point to diseases like post‑streptococcal GN or lupus nephritis.

faq.q: Can a patient have nephrotic syndrome without a kidney biopsy?
faq.a: Yes, if clinical features (massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema) and serology strongly suggest a specific disease, treatment may start while biopsy is arranged.

faq.q: What is the role of ACE inhibitors in glomerular disease?
faq.a: They lower intraglomerular pressure, reduce proteinuria, and slow progression of chronic kidney disease.

exam: Describe how you would differentiate nephrotic from nephritic syndrome using urine findings and clinical signs.
List the primary causes of adult nephrotic syndrome and the key diagnostic test for each.
Explain why ACE inhibitors are recommended for all patients with proteinuric glomerular disease.
